title: O Thou Whom Fain My Soul Would Love
description: O Thou Whom Fain My Soul Would Love in Tonic Solfa to SELENA, doh is Ab: the solfa with the words, staff notation, 3 verses and a piano.
about: John Wesley printed these words in A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780), hymn 113. They first appeared in a book he and his brother Charles published together, and the Collection's own index cannot say which of the two wrote them.
The book printed the words without tunes. They are in Long Metre, six lines (8.8.8.8.8.8), and this page sets them to SELENA; any other Long Metre, six lines tune fits them as well.
underlay: O thou whom fain my soul would love! Whom I would glad-ly die to know; This veil of un-be-lief re-move, And show me, all thy good-ness show; Je-sus, thy-self in me re-veal, Tell me thy name, thy na-ture tell.

lines: O thou whom fain my soul would love!
Whom I would gladly die to know;
And show me, all thy goodness show;
Tell me thy name, thy nature tell.
Hast thou been with me, Lord, so long,
Yet thee, my Lord, have I not known?
I claim thee with a faltering tongue,
I pray thee, in a feeble groan,
Tell me, O tell me, who thou art,
And speak thy name into my heart!
If now thou talkest by the way
With such an abject worm as me,
Open mine eyes that I may see,
That I may understand thy word,
And now cry out - "It is the Lord!"

source: John Wesley, A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780)
licence: Public domain: Charles Wesley died in 1788; John Wesley died in 1791.
credits: Words by Charles Wesley (1707–1788) or John Wesley (1703–1791), public domain, as printed in John Wesley's Collection of Hymns (1780); set to SELENA by NoteFusion, as words-only hymn books were sung.
